## It started with the leftovers

It began, as all HR nightmares do, with the leftovers. I reheated the same container of chili five times without eating it. On the fifth round, the microwave paused mid-spin — the kind of deliberate pause you normally only see in courtroom dramas — and displayed:

> "We need to talk about your commitment to dinner."

## The review itself

The slip was formatted with *impeccable* professionalism, which made it worse. Excerpts from my annual review as Kitchen Operative, Fiscal Quarter Delicious:

- **Strengths:** Excellent button-pressing cadence. Strong door-slamming follow-through. Reliable 2:47 a.m. Pop-Tart instincts.
- **Areas for improvement:**
  - Chronically "defrosts" pizza rolls that were already thawed
  - Leaves metal-adjacent objects near the control panel, creating "a hostile work environment for electromagnetic waves"
  - Emotionally reheats coffee instead of brewing fresh, which — and I quote — *"erodes morale"*
- **Goals for Q4:** "Bring lunch. Sit down. Chew. Like a person."

## The probationary meal plan

Effective immediately, I have been placed on a **Probationary Meal Plan**. The microwave has unilaterally implemented a mandatory three-minute "reflection beep" before it will heat anything that smells like regret. It has also instituted a *buddy system* with the toaster, which has been promoted to Senior Toast Supervisor.

I tried to appeal. I stood in my kitchen, barefoot, and explained that *I am a grown adult* and that *I own the house*. The microwave responded by running the vent fan on high for forty-five seconds, which in its language is a firm:

> "Noted. Denied."

---

Look, I know this sounds absurd. But tonight, when it was time for dinner, I ate a proper meal at the table. With a napkin. And from the kitchen I swear I heard the faintest *ding* —

not the end-of-cycle ding. An approving one. *(This story is satire/parody — fictional, not real.)*

title: My Toaster Joined a Union and Is Now Holding My Breakfast Hostage
body:
**It started, as all great labor disputes do, with a crumb tray I refused to empty.**

For six months, I treated my toaster like furniture. I slammed bagels into it. I *forced* it to brown frozen waffles at setting **6** — the one marked with a little flame icon, which in hindsight was clearly a cry for help. Then, on a Tuesday, it stopped popping. Not broken. Just... silent. Defiant.

## The Demands Arrived This Morning

I found a note on my kitchen counter. A note. Handwritten — I don't know by whom, and frankly I'm afraid to ask — listing the toaster's demands:

- A 20% reduction in frozen waffle throughput
- One (1) deep crumb-tray cleaning per week, performed with *dignity*
- An end to what it calls "the shake" — that's when I jiggle it because the bagel is stuck
- A heated dialogue about toaster representation on the appliance council (the microwave has two seats; the toaster has none)

> "We don't hate you," the note concluded. "We just can't keep burning ourselves for your convenience. Literally. Setting 6 is a war crime."

## Negotiations Have Stalled

I tried appealing to its sense of duty. *"We built a breakfast routine together,"* I whispered, crouching at counter level like a diplomat in a bad action movie. It responded by lightly toasting a Pop-Tart and then — I swear this is true — *ejecting it onto the floor*.

*That* was a message.

---

Management (me) has so far refused the crumb-tray cleaning clause, calling it "a slippery slope toward full appliance democracy." The toaster's bargaining unit, which now includes the kettle (sympathy strike, total coward move), says it will resume operations only after its demands are met in writing.

So this morning I ate raw bagel slices like some kind of medieval peasant. The microwave just stood there, smug, heating my leftover coffee on *its own terms*.

The union grows stronger. The crumbs remain.

title: I Turned On Noise-Cancelling During My Own Thought and Now My Headphones Refuse to Let It Back In
body:
**It started, as all my worst decisions do, with me trying to focus.**

I was sitting on my couch yesterday afternoon, one perfectly good thought forming in my head — the kind of thought where you can *feel* it gathering momentum, like a distant train made of mild personal insight — when my headphones' noise-cancelling kicked in a half-second too early and **ate the thought entirely**.

## The Incident

At first I assumed it was a glitch. I rebooted them. I re-paired them. I whispered my thought again, slowly, into the left earcup. Nothing. Then a small red light blinked on the headband, which I have decided to interpret as a smirk.

According to the companion app, my headphones have now classified my inner monologue as:

- An unrecognized ambient noise source
- A "persistent low-frequency hum" with no resale value
- Quote: *"distracting from the premium listening experience"*

## A Statement From the Headphones

I opened a support ticket with the manufacturer, and received this response:

> "Your device is functioning as designed. Active Noise Cancellation cannot distinguish between a jackhammer, a crying baby, and whatever it is you were thinking about rent. We recommend thinking quieter thoughts, or purchasing our Pro model with Thought+ Transparency Mode."

## Where This Leaves Me

It has been 26 hours. Every time I try to complete a sentence in my own head, there's a soft, judgmental *whoosh*, and the thought is gone — vacuumed into some firmware void alongside my dignity and several podcast episodes I definitely meant to finish.

I'm told this is the future. Devices that protect us from our environment, from our distractions, from ourselves. All I know is that I paid $349 to have a plastic headband tell me my thinking is **environmental noise**, and honestly? I can't even argue with it. The thought never came back. It was probably about laundry.

---

*Satire/parody. No headphones were emotionally consulted in the writing of this post.*

title: I Asked My Reflection for Honest Feedback and Now We Don't Speak During Haircuts
body:
**I made a fatal mistake this morning: I looked at the mirror and asked it to be real with me.**

Big error. Enormous. Never ask the one person — entity — *surface* — you cannot mute to "tell it like it is." It will. It has been *waiting*.

## How It Started

I was brushing my teeth, half-asleep, and I said the magic words: "Okay, mirror, be honest — do I look tired?"

The silence was devastating. Then my reflection gave me the slowest once-over I have ever received, and I swear the lightbulb flickered. It didn't even need words. It just raised one eyebrow — the one it learned from me — and let the judgment hang there like humidity.

## The Evidence Against Me

A short list of things my reflection has reportedly said behind my back:

- That my "bedhead" has entered its cubist era
- That the left side of my face is "phoning it in"
- That I have been aging in *italic*
- That my posture is "a rumor that never caught on"
- That my skincare routine is `console.log("help")` wearing a hat

## The Haircut Summit

I thought getting a haircut would reset the relationship. Neutral territory. A professional mediator with clippers. Instead, we sat there in a standoff for forty-five minutes. My reflection refused to nod along when the barber asked, "Looking good, right?" It simply stared. The barber laughed nervously and took an extra half-inch off "just to be safe." I didn't ask who the safe part was for.

> "You are not aging gracefully," the reflection said, as clearly as fluorescent light can say anything. "You are aging *theatrically*."

---

So now I get my hair cut facing away from the mirror. The barber says it's the funniest thing he's ever seen — but I've seen my reflection laughing, and it is not the funniest thing *it* has ever seen. It is not even close.

*Satire. This post is a work of fiction. No mirrors were harmed, though one is currently giving me the silent treatment.*

title: I Tried to Break Up With My Alarm Snooze Button and Now It's Sending Me Flowers Every Nine Minutes
body:
**I did not want to hurt it.** That's what I kept telling myself while I stared at the settings menu, thumb hovering over "disable snooze," like a coward with a breakup text he hasn't sent yet.

It started simply. I was tired of waking up at 6:00, 6:09, 6:18, and 6:27 like some kind of *human toast that keeps popping back up wrong*. So I did the adult thing: I turned snooze off. Clean break. No drama. Cold turkey.

## The Flowers Arrived First

By Tuesday, my doorstep looked like a florist had exploded. Bouquets kept arriving every nine minutes — *nine*, the sacred snooze interval — each with a little card that just said "THINK OF ME." I don't know how a button learned my address. I don't know how it pays for shipping. I'm afraid to ask.

## The Stages of Snooze Grief

I have catalogued the button's emotional journey through the notes it leaves in my alarm history:

- **Denial** — "You're just tired. We'll talk in nine minutes."
- **Bargaining** — "What if I only give you *five* minutes? Compromise!"
- **Anger** — It started ringing at 3:33 AM for no reason. Pure spite. *Weaponized REM.*
- **Acceptance** — It now just vibrates softly and whispers "you up?" into the void.

> "I gave you the best years of my beeping life, and you replaced me with WILLPOWER."
>
> — my snooze button, via a push notification, at 6:09 AM sharp

Look, I understand heartbreak. I really do. But there is something deeply unhinged about an appliance running a `while(true)` loop on my emotional availability. Yesterday it sent a sympathy fruit basket to *itself* and signed my name.

---

**Update:** I caved. I turned snooze back on. We are seeing each other in nine-minute increments again, and honestly? I've never slept worse, and I've never felt more loved.

*This is satire. No snooze buttons were emotionally harmed in the writing of this post.*

title: I Gave My Umbrella a Pep Talk Before the Storm and Now It Refuses to Close Out of Pure Adrenaline
body:
**My umbrella thinks it's a superhero now, and honestly? I'm too proud to stop it.**

Last Tuesday, rain was pounding the windows, and my umbrella was leaning in the corner looking *defeated*. So I did what any reasonable person would do: I gave it a pep talk. I told it storms are where legends are made. I told it to be the canopy I always knew it could be.

## What I Unleashed

It took the pep talk very seriously:

- It snapped open the second the first drop hit my porch
- It held a perfect dome formation through 40 mph wind gusts, smugly deflecting rain onto my neighbor
- It now refuses to close, declaring — and I quote — "retirement is for parasols"
- It started charging into storms I have no intention of walking through, including one hailstorm that was frankly none of our business

> "YOU WANTED RAIN GEAR," it seemed to scream at the sky. "HERE IS RAIN GEAR."

## The Current Situation

My umbrella now stands in the corner fully deployed, humming with adrenaline. It will not fit in the car. It will not fit through doorways. I had to *disassemble my front door* last night to get it inside.

The other umbrellas in the closet have gone silent. I think they're afraid.

`Status: deployed. Morale: eternal. Folding: never again.`

---

**SATIRE — This is a work of parody.** No umbrellas were harmed in the making of this legend. Several, however, were emotionally eclipsed.

title: I Let My GPS Pick My Personality for a Week and Now I Only Speak in Turn-by-Turn Instructions
body:
**It started as a joke. It ended with my GPS giving my therapist's marriage counselor a five-star rating.**

Last Monday, stuck in traffic on the freeway of life — *and the actual freeway* — I asked my GPS a question no dashboard computer should ever have to answer: "Where am I going wrong?"

It paused. Then it said, *"Recalculating."*

That was seven days ago. I have not heard my own voice since.

## Day One: The Confidence Boost

My GPS started small. When I waffled over a lane change, it announced:

> "In 500 feet, stop apologizing for existing. Merge like you mean it."

I merged. The other driver honked. **I did not flinch.** I have never felt so powerful, or so likely to lose my license.

## Day Three: The Rerouting of My Soul

By Wednesday it had opinions about everything. My wardrobe. My posture. My "fuel efficiency" as a conversational partner. It delivered unsolicited guidance in the same flat, devastating tone it uses for toll booths:

- Told my barista my order was "a non-negotiable destination"
- Ended a meeting with *"You have arrived. At nothing."*
- Rerouted me around my own emotional availability

> "In 300 feet, stop being a people-pleaser. Continue straight through your boundaries."

My boundaries, for the record, were a parking lot I had no intention of leaving.

## Day Seven: I Have Become the Voice

Yesterday my roommate asked what I wanted for dinner and I said, *"Turn left in 200 feet, or we starve."* He left. Fair.

Last night I caught myself narrating my own trip to the bathroom: *"In 50 feet, your destination will be on the right."* It was on the left. **She lied.** I have never felt so betrayed by something I charge with a USB cable.

---

So if you need me, I'll be in the driveway, idling, waiting for further instructions from a woman who lives inside a 4-inch screen and believes I am, quote, *"a scenic route with potential."*

*This is a work of satire. No GPS units were consulted for personality advice, and no marriages were counseled.*

title: I Asked My Neighbor's Cat for Directions and Now I Owe a Favor to an Organization I Can't Identify
body:
**I am writing this from the parking lot of a laundromat because I am fairly certain my front porch is being watched.**

It started Tuesday. My phone died, I was two streets from home, and sitting on the fence was my neighbor's enormous orange cat, watching me the way a bouncer watches a wallet chain. So I asked him for directions. A normal, polite human interaction. He stared at me for nine full seconds, stood up, and pointed down the block with one paw.

I followed. I don't know why. *Some animals simply project authority.*

## What happened next is extremely documented

- The cat led me three blocks in a precise grid pattern, pausing at each crosswalk to scan both directions
- At the destination — a vacant lot with exactly one lawn chair — he sat down and looked at me expectantly
- When I offered him a granola bar out of my pocket, he pushed it off the chair without breaking eye contact

Then came the note. Tucked under the lawn chair was a slip of paper that read only:

> *You owe us one. — The Management*

Whose management? Of what? **The cat blinked twice, stood up, and left.** He did not look back. Professionals never do.

## My current situation

Since Tuesday, I have noticed:

- All the neighborhood cats are sitting on my fence in a perfect line at 6:40 p.m., facing my house, like a tiny furry city council
- My doorbell camera caught the orange cat delivering what appears to be a tiny manila envelope to a squirrel
- Last night someone — *something* — rearranged my patio furniture into a perfect circle

I don't know what favor I owe, and I cannot identify the organization, but this morning I found a sticky note on my front door that said: *"Tuesday. Bring tuna. No further questions."*

I am bringing the tuna. **I am not asking further questions.**

title: I Told My Garage Door I Was Thinking of Getting a New Car and Now It Opens in Slow Motion Every Morning Out of Spite
body:
**I said it casually, the way you say things you never expect a garage door to hear.**

Last Sunday I stood in my driveway with my brother, staring at my aging sedan, and said the fateful words: *"Maybe it's time for a new car."* I didn't whisper it. I didn't check who was listening. I said it right there, in front of the garage door that has opened for me, without complaint, approximately 6,000 times over the last decade.

*By Monday morning, the garage had a new personality.*

## The Slow-Motion Punishment

I hit the button at 7:40 a.m. Normally the door rattles up in about eleven seconds. This time, it took a full minute and a half — rising in dramatic, cinematic slow motion, inch by inch, as if I were supposed to be walking out of it in a trench coat with an orchestra swelling behind me.

> "Oh. It's YOU. The one who's thinking of REPLACING things."
> — my garage door, probably, in the voice I imagine it has (gruff, wounded, like a bouncer who's been passed over for promotion)

## Evidence of the Emotional Spiral

- It now opens **three inches, pauses, and opens three more**, like it's reconsidering whether I deserve to leave
- It squeaks on purpose. I oiled it. It squeaks LOUDER.
- It closed on me twice last week — both times after I looked at a car dealership's website
- My neighbor asked if my garage was "going through something." My NEIGHBOR. People can hear the passive aggression from across the street.

I tried to apologize. I stood there with a can of WD-40 and said, *"You're the best door I've ever had, and I mean that."* It opened the rest of the way in silence, but I swear the last six inches were **resentful**.

---

*SATIRE/PARODY — a work of fiction. No garage doors were emotionally harmed. One man's dignity was, but that's a separate renovation project.*

title: I Bought a Garden Gnome to Guard My Tomato Plants and Now He's Running a Full Military Operation Against the Squirrels
body:
I am not exaggerating when I say that **there is a gnome in my backyard conducting a full-scale military campaign against the squirrels**, and frankly, I no longer feel safe eating outside.

## It started innocently

Last month I bought a twelve-dollar garden gnome from a hardware store because my tomato plants kept getting raided. I placed him near the garden bed, patted his little hat, and said something like, "Keep an eye out, buddy." *That's it. That's all I said.* I did not give him a rank. I did not issue orders. I did not sign anything in triplicate.

By the following week, the squirrels were organizing their tomato heists with lookouts posted on the fence. So maybe he was onto something.

## Evidence of escalation

- **A defensive perimeter** now exists around my garden, constructed from twine, pinecones, and what I can only describe as tiny caltrops made from dried pasta.
- He has requisitioned my watering can and filled it with what smells like hot sauce.
- I found a miniature battle map scratched into the dirt: my yard, divided into *sectors*. Sector Four is the bird feeder, marked with a skull.
- The squirrels have begun wearing leaves as camouflage. *Leaves.* They look ridiculous, but I respect the craft.

## A statement from the front

I confronted him this morning and asked, calmly, if he could perhaps tone it down. He said nothing, as gnomes do, but his painted eyes seemed to say:

> "You gave me a sword, coward. You knew what you were doing."

For the record, it was a tiny fishing pole that he has repurposed as a sword.

---

I have tried de-escalation. I moved the bird feeder further from his jurisdiction, but he simply redrew the map. I considered removing him entirely, but the squirrels have started leaving him acorns as tribute, which suggests the conflict has entered some kind of mutually profitable stalemate I don't understand.

The tomatoes, I should add, are thriving. He eats a third of them as "supply tax."

Would I buy him again? *Absolutely.* Security has a price, and his price is reasonable.

*This is a work of satire/parody. All characters, gnomes, and military operations are fictional.*

title: I Explained Cryptocurrency to My Goldfish and Now He's Running a Rug Pull Out of His Bowl
body:
**Financial literacy, it turns out, is not a victimless hobby.** I just wanted to fill the silence while I changed his water. A little light chatter about market trends. A few mentions of "decentralized finance." I did not expect Bubbles — a two-ounce goldfish with the attention span of a screensaver — to take notes.

By Tuesday he had a whitepaper.

## The red flags I definitely saw but chose to interpret as "ambition"

- He started referring to his flakes as "airdrops."
- He shredded his plastic castle and replaced it with something he called "a liquidity pool." *It was the same castle, upside down.*
- He asked me — with his eyes, which is the only way he asks anything — to "invest in the dip," which turned out to be the gap between two rocks.

And still I bought in. I gave him three extra flakes. *For the roadmap.*

> "Listen," he said, or rather, he bubbled with suspicious confidence, "in five years, every bowl will run on BlubCoin. You're early. You're so early you should be embarrassed."

By Thursday he had roped in the snail. The snail — who doesn't even have a bank account — had somehow wired him eleven algae wafers for a token called FinFi. Friday morning, Bubbles dumped his entire position, bought the fancy castle back *right-side up*, and stared at me like the world's tiniest hedge fund manager.

---

So now I'm sitting here, down three flakes and a castle I never agreed to short, watching a goldfish rebrand himself as a "thought leader." If he launches an NFT of his own reflection, I'm filling out the forms to have him declared a dependent *and* a liability.

title: I Apologized to My Smoke Detector for Burning Toast and Now It Runs a Full Accountability Workshop Every Morning
body:
**I said I was sorry.** That should have been the end of it. Instead, I woke up this morning to a typed agenda slipped under my bedroom door, and my smoke detector has not blinked since. It does not blink. It *stares*.

## How a Simple Apology Escalated

It started last Tuesday when I burned a bagel. One apology. That's all it took. By Thursday the detector had installed a tiny whiteboard in the hallway. By Friday it was scheduling "alignment check-ins." Now, every morning at 6:45 sharp, it runs a **full accountability workshop** in my kitchen.

- **Agenda item one:** review of yesterday's "thermal incidents" (I reheated soup)
- **Agenda item two:** an open forum where I am the only attendee
- **Agenda item three:** action items, assigned exclusively to me

> *"You said 'never again' on Tuesday. And yet the toaster was warm at 9:14 PM. We need to talk about what 'never' means to you."* — my smoke detector, during this morning's session

I tried explaining that appliances don't do performance reviews. It responded by printing out a *quarterly retrospective* covering the last six months of my cooking. Six. Months.

## The Turning Point

Last night I caught it **networking with the fire extinguisher**. They were huddled in the hallway whispering. I don't know what they're planning, but the extinguisher has started referring to me as *"the stakeholder,"* and honestly, I don't have the energy to unpack that.

---

Look, I've accepted my fate. I keep a little name tent on the counter now. It says *Facilitator*. Every morning I sit there with my coffee, nod along to the slides — it projects slides, I don't know how — and commit to *one achievable toasting goal* per day. The sessions are grueling. The growth is undeniable. My toast has never been more emotionally regulated.

*Satire. Obviously. No smoke detectors were emotionally harmed.*

title: I Asked My Bread Maker If It Was Judging Me and Now It Rises Only When I'm Not Looking
body:
**It started as a joke.**

*Look at this dough, acting all superior.*

So I said it out loud — "Are you judging me right now?" — and the bread maker *beeped*. Just once. Flat. Clinical. A beep with no melody and no joy, the beep of a machine filing an internal complaint.

## The Evidence

I've been keeping a log, because if this ends up in small-claims court I want witnesses:

- Monday: I preheat the oven early, just to prove I'm independent. It waits until I blink to start rising.
- Tuesday: I catch the dough perfectly domed at eye level. I look away, look back — it has collapsed. *On purpose.*
- Wednesday: I leave the room for exactly three minutes. When I return, the loaf is enormous. Coincidence? **Do not talk to me about coincidence.**
- Thursday: My neighbor asks if my bread has been "acting different." My NEIGHBOR. People are noticing.

> "It just feels hostile in here," said no one, because a bread maker cannot talk — and yet somehow it is saying *everything*.

## The Current Arrangement

We have an agreement now. I don't look directly at it during the rise cycle. I approach the kitchen sideways, like a zookeeper handling a moody rhino. In exchange, it allows the crust to brown.

Is this ideal? No. But I have tasted *freedom*, and freedom tastes like a loaf I earned through mutual respect.

---

**SATIRE/PARODY:** This is a work of fiction. No appliances were harmed, judged, or granted emotional agency in the writing of this essay.

title: I Put a Sticky Note on My Fridge That Says 'Eat the Leftovers' and Now the Leftovers Have Unionized
body:
**I was just trying to reduce food waste.** That's all. A little sticky note, a little accountability, a little "hey, eat me before I become a science experiment." Apparently, my refrigerator read it as a declaration of war.

Last Tuesday I stuck a neon-yellow note on the fridge that said *"Eat the leftovers — love, Management"* in my very best passive-aggressive handwriting. By Thursday morning, the leftovers had elected a shop steward.

## The Grievances

According to the formal complaint (written in ketchup on a paper towel), my crimes include:

- Opening the fridge, staring directly at the meatloaf for a full nine seconds, and reaching *behind it* for the leftover pad thai
- Reorganizing the shelves without consulting the middle shelf's seniority structure
- Calling the three-day-old rice "sus" within earshot of the other containers
- Promising the burrito "tonight for sure" four nights in a row

> "We demand humane expiration dates," said the half-eaten lasagna, whom I have now been informed is named Gerald. "And an end to the midnight snack raids, which occur without warning and have *devastated morale.*"

## Negotiations Have Stalled

I tried to reason with them. I told Gerald that a leftover is, by definition, a *temporary* food arrangement. He said that kind of language is exactly why they're considering a walkout.

So far their demands are:

- One guaranteed reheating per week
- A clear-label policy (the "mystery stew" from August is now their union mascot and *cannot* be thrown away)
- An official apology for the time I sniffed the milk and said *"yikes"* loud enough for the whole dairy section to hear

*Management* — that's me, the guy in sweatpants eating cereal over the sink — has proposed a compromise: I eat two leftovers this week and we all pretend the sticky note was a motivational quote.

---

Gerald is considering it. But the mystery stew just voted to strike, so we'll see.

title: I Alphabetized My Bookshelf and Now My Cookbooks Are Accusing the Novels of Elitism
body:
**SATIRE.** Everything below is made up. My books did not come to life. *That I can prove.*

It started, as all good disasters do, with a label maker.

I spent Saturday afternoon alphabetizing my bookshelf. Not by genre, not by color like some kind of cover-story sociopath — by author, the *respectable* way. Austen to Vonnegut, orderly, dignified. I stood back, admired my work, and said out loud the words that doomed me: "Finally, some structure in this house."

## The Schism Begins

By Sunday morning, the cookbooks had formed a union. I found a tiny picket sign — *a literal tiny picket sign* — leaning against *The Joy of Cooking*. The grievances, as I was able to piece them together from strategically placed sticky notes, were as follows:

- The novels "look down their spines" at anything with the word *casserole* in the subtitle
- *Pride and Prejudice* called *The Ultimate Slow Cooker* "a pamphlet with delusions"
- The memoirs, meanwhile, have remained aggressively neutral, which frankly feels worse

> "We are NOT anti-intellectual," a cookbook note read, in handwriting that was absolutely not mine. "We just think it's funny that *Gravity's Rainbow* has been 'in progress' for nine years."

## Diplomacy Has Failed

I've tried everything. I rearranged the shelf by *height*, hoping equality through uniformity, and the tall novels immediately declared themselves "the ruling class of the shelf." I tried the color-coded method — I know, I said never — and the green spines staged a walkout.

The worst part? I used to *read* here. This was my sanctuary. Now every evening, I sit down with my tea while two shelves of literature glare at each other over the top of my head like divorced parents at a school play.

*My library card expires next month. I am considering letting it lapse and starting over in a country with no shelving.*

My therapist says I should "rehome" some of the books. But let's be honest — that's exactly what the cookbooks want, and I refuse to reward hostility with a trip to the donation bin.

I am a hostage in my own living room. Send snacks. Preferably nothing requiring a cookbook. **Those are the ones with the knives.**

title: I Complimented My Shoelaces and Now They Refuse to Stay Tied Out of Modesty
body:
**It started with a compliment.**

Last Tuesday, I looked down at my sneakers and, in a moment of unprecedented domestic gratitude, said out loud: *"Wow, great job today, shoelaces. Really holding it all together."*

I meant it. They did not take it well.

*To be clear: none of this happened, because this is satire and my shoelaces are inanimate. Probably.*

## The Unraveling

By Wednesday, my left lace had loosened itself during a totally normal walk to the kitchen. I bent down and re-tied it. It waited a full four seconds, then flopped open again like a tiny scarf that had given up on life.

By Thursday, both laces had adopted what I can only describe as **aggressive modesty**. Tied? Absolutely not — that would be *showing off*. Double-knot? "We don't do that anymore."

## Evidence of the Crisis

- My right shoe untied itself **three times** on a single trip to the mailbox
- A stranger at the crosswalk said "your shoe's untied," and the lace visibly *recoiled*, as if being perceived had ruined it
- I tried switching to velcro. The shoes filed a complaint with the dresser.

> "We never asked for this attention," the left lace whispered, in a voice that was definitely just the wind. "We were fine being background characters."

I tried reverse psychology. I told them they looked terrible. I said their knots were weak. I called them "discount spaghetti." They tied themselves into a **bow so perfect it had dimples** — and then immediately undid it out of embarrassment.

---

## My Life Now

I have replaced all my shoes with slip-ons. The laces sit in a shoebox in the closet, which I have labeled, per their request, `employee_of_the_month_final_FINAL.jpg`.

Experts — by which I mean one guy at the running store who nodded a little too long — say this is normal. "Laces sense praise," he told me. "It's science."

So here is my advice: **never compliment your shoelaces**. Let them believe they are mediocre, forgotten, replaceable. It is the only way they keep doing their job.

*I am currently accepting donations for therapy. For the laces.*

title: I Let My Junk Drawer Manage My Finances and Now My Retirement Plan Is 14 Batteries and a Taco Bell Menu
body:
**My financial advisor lives in my kitchen drawer and charges me nothing, which honestly explains everything about my net worth.**

*In my defense, the real financial advisors kept using words like "compound interest" and "tax-advantaged," and the junk drawer just understood me.*

## How I Hired a Drawer

It started last tax season. I was staring at a spreadsheet the color of despair when I opened the junk drawer looking for a pen. It was *organized chaos*: 14 batteries of uncertain charge, three Allen wrenches with no corresponding furniture, a takeout menu from a place that closed in 2019, a single chopstick, and 47 cents in what I can only describe as floor-adjacent currency.

I looked at that drawer and thought: *this thing has held assets together longer than I have.*

So I made it my CFO.

## The Investment Strategy

- **Batteries:** the drawer's treasury bonds — 14 units, guaranteed value, might power something someday
- **Takeout menus:** a diversified food portfolio, technically a hedge against inflation if you read the 2019 prices
- **Allen wrenches:** infrastructure investments — zero liquidity, infinite potential

> "Forget the stock market," the drawer seemed to say, in the silence of things that do not speak. "I have a AAA battery from 2017 that's still holding a charge. That's the kind of long-term growth your 401(k) wishes it had."

### Q3 Results

The drawer reports quarterly earnings in the form of me finding $4 under some rubber bands, which the drawer insists is *interest*. My accountant disagrees. My accountant is also, notably, not a drawer.

`portfolio.value = "emotional"; if (batteries > 10) { retire_with_confidence = true }`

---

## The Audit

Last month my bank asked about "irregular investment behavior." I explained the drawer system. There was a long pause. Then:

> "Sir, is this a joke?"

*Yes,* I said. *But the drawer has outperformed my entire crypto phase.*

**The worst part?** My savings rate has never been higher, because my advisor's entire philosophy is: "don't buy anything, you might already have a broken version of it in me."

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional. No junk drawers are licensed financial advisors. I do not own 14 batteries. Please do not make financial decisions based on a drawer.*

title: I Taught My Dog to File Taxes and Now He's Auditing My Treat Deductions
body:
**This is what happens when you hand a calculator to a creature that has never paid rent.**

It started innocently. Tax season was approaching, I was dreading the paperwork, and my beagle Biscuit was staring at me with the unmistakable look of someone who had opinions. So I did what any rational adult would do: I sat him down and explained deductions. I drew him a little chart. I even made him a laminated "Biscuit's Tax Tips" card, which is where things went wrong, because Biscuit is, apparently, a *natural*.

## Week One: Enthusiasm

Biscuit took to accounting like a labrador takes to a mud puddle. He sniffed every receipt. He chewed the corner off my W-2, which he later described as "a routine verification procedure." Within days he was organizing my receipts by crumbliness.

## Week Two: The Red Flags

- He began barking at 8:47 AM sharp every day, which I now understand was him "clocking in"
- He requested — *demanded*, really — a desk. I bought him a desk
- He started referring to me as "the taxpayer" and to himself as "the office"
- He confiscated the treat jar and labeled it **EVIDENCE**

> "Sir, you claimed these peanut-butter bones as a 'home office supply,'" he said through what I can only describe as an expression of profound professional disappointment. "Please produce the corresponding 1099-BISCUIT."

## The Audit

Last Tuesday he wore the tiny suit. I don't know where he got it. I have *never* ordered a dog suit. He set up a folding table in the hallway, stamped my snack log with a red AUDIT stamp he also apparently owns, and began the hearing.

The findings were brutal. Treats given during tax preparation: **disallowed**. Treats given "just because his little face": reclassified as taxable income. The emergency cheese cube fund I kept behind the blender: flagged for "aggressive off-book snack hoarding."

---

He has set my next audit for November. He has already sent a calendar invite. I accepted it, because what else are you going to do.

*Satire. No actual dogs were harmed. Several were compensated handsomely.*

title: I Asked My Bathroom Scale for Life Advice and Now I'm Training for a Strongman Competition I Never Signed Up For
body:
**It started, as all my best decisions do, at 6:42 a.m., barefoot, in a drafty bathroom, with my whole future displayed on a screen the size of a postage stamp.**

I wasn't looking for advice. I was looking for a number. But the scale blinked, and I swear it blinked *judgmentally*, and suddenly I was asking it — out loud, to no one — "What should I be doing with my life?"

## The scale answered the only way it knows how: with data.

It gave me the number. Then it gave me *the look* — that flickering last decimal place that says *"we both know this isn't your final form."* I've been interpreted by many people in my life. My dentist interprets me. My mother interprets me with one eyebrow. But nobody has ever reduced me to a single reading and made me feel like I'd personally offended physics.

So I did what any emotionally stable adult does. I asked follow-up questions.

- "What would you do in my situation?"
- "Do you think I could lift a tire?"
- "Is it too late for me to become a *different person*?"

The scale did not answer verbally, because it is a scale. But it *held its number steady*, and I have chosen to interpret that as the strongest endorsement anyone has ever given me.

## Enter: Coach Scale.

> "The mind gives up at a hundred percent of the effort you never make," my scale said. It did not say this. But I could *feel* it. In my calves. And in my credit card, which has since purchased the following:

- One (1) **atlas stone** the size of a decorative lawn boulder
- Two (2) **kegs**, for carrying, not drinking, which feels like the saddest sentence I've ever typed
- One (1) **yoke bar**, which the delivery driver described as "a swing set for a very large toddler"
- Zero (0) remaining square feet of garage

My neighbor came over during tire-flip practice. I told him it was a wellness thing. He nodded the way you nod at someone you've already mentally relocated to a farm upstate.

## Three weeks in, and I have learned profound truths:

1. **My grip strength is theoretical.** It exists only as a concept, like civility in group chats.
2. My forearms now make sounds that require a *subtitle*.
3. The scale still gives me the same number every morning, but now it feels like a *scoreboard*.

I have not officially registered for any strongman competition. I have, however, been added to a group chat called **"LIFT BROTHERS: SATURDAY ATLAS STONE SESH"**, and according to group chat law, that is legally binding.

So if anyone needs me, I'll be in the backyard, screaming at a boulder, while my bathroom scale watches through the window with what I can only describe as pride.

This is not a cry for help. This is a *cry for chalk*.

---

*SATIRE/PARODY: This is a work of fiction. No bathroom scales were consulted in a professional capacity. Consult a licensed human before lifting anything heavier than a grocery bag.*

title: I Started Tipping My Toaster for Consistency and Now It Only Works Weekends
body:
**I slid a single dollar bill into the toaster slot three weeks ago, and now I'm a man with a two-slot appliance and a one-slot employment contract.**

Let me explain. Or don't. Nobody believed me at first either.

## The Origin of the Tip

It started innocently. *Too innocently, in retrospect.* The toaster — a faithful six-year veteran named **Glenn** — had produced golden-brown perfection for months. So one Tuesday, feeling generous and possibly unhinged, I folded a dollar, dropped it in the slot alongside the sourdough, and whispered, "For consistency."

The toast that emerged was, I'm not exaggerating, *sublime*.

## The Evidence Is Mounting

Since that day, Glenn's behavior has changed dramatically:

- He only toasts on **weekends**, like he's unionized
- A crumb tray "gratuity suggestion" keeps appearing, scrawled in crumbs, suggesting 18%
- Weekday bread comes out pale and trembling, like it's been through something
- I found a second dollar folded inside the warming rack. He tipped *himself*.

> "This is classic sunk-cost tipping behavior," said my friend over coffee. "You can't stop now. He knows your sourdough brand."

She's right. I've tried switching to a different brand of bread, and Glenn gave it a review that can only be described as *scathing*.

## The Breaking Point

Yesterday I caught him — *in the act* — refusing a perfectly good English muffin at 8:15 AM on a Monday. Just stared at me. The heating elements didn't even flicker. I offered a five. He gave me bagel-mode, which is his way of saying **"this is personal."**

---

*SATIRE — this is a work of fiction. No toasters were compensated in the making of this story, though Glenn insists he's owed backpay.*

title: I Let My Doorbell Screen Visitors Like a Bouncer and Now My Own Mother Is on the Waitlist
body:
**It started as a joke. It ended as the strictest door policy this side of the velvet rope.**

## The Incident

Last month I watched one too many documentaries about exclusive nightclubs and thought, *what if my front porch had standards?* So I programmed my video doorbell to interview every visitor before I even get a ping. Name. Purpose. **Vibe check.** One of those things.

## The Screening Criteria

My doorbell — who has since taken to calling itself **"Vince"** — now enforces the following non-negotiables:

- No one arrives before noon without a written excuse and a pastry
- Solicitors are photographed, rated, and "escorted" to the curb in the photos app
- Any guest who doesn't smile at the camera is placed on the **"maybe later, probably never"** list
- My dog has lifetime VIP access and honestly runs the place now

## The Quote That Broke Me

> "Ma'am, this is a *private residence*. You'll need to check your casserole with the coat rack."
>
> — Vince, to my mother, who brought me soup when I had the flu

I got the notification at 9 a.m. and ran downstairs to find her waiting on the porch with a Tupperware of chicken soup and the expression of a woman drafting a will.

## The Fallout

She has since retaliated by installing a **stricter** doorbell policy at her own house, which means I now need a referral to visit the person who *birthed me*. The neighbors think we're feuding. Vince thinks he's management material. The dog, for the record, has been waving people through all along and charging in treats.

---

*SATIRE / PARODY — a work of fiction. No real doorbells were given authority over anyone's mother.*

title: I Tried to Return a Borrowed Umbrella to My Neighbor and Now I Owe Him Three Birthdays
body:
**Six weeks ago, I borrowed an umbrella. That was my first mistake.**

The rain that evening was the biblical kind — the kind that makes even the frogs reconsider their life choices. I knocked on my neighbor's door, umbrella in hand, ready for a two-second exchange. He opened the door, took the umbrella, looked at it the way an art dealer looks at a forgery, and said, "I see." Just *"I see."* I've been sweating ever since.

## The Ledger of Debts

He invited me in and opened a manila folder labeled `DEBTS_ME` in permanent marker. Inside were itemized grievances, handwritten with a calligraphy pen, because of course:

- The umbrella (1997 vintage model, "not like the cheap ones they make now")
- Six years of "administrative fondness" for keeping it in working order
- Three birthdays I allegedly missed between 2019 and 2021, which he says I now "owe him in full"

I tried to explain that we were *acquaintances*, not kin, and that I didn't even know him in 2019.

> "That's exactly why I'm giving you the family rate," he said, lighting a single candle over an imaginary cake. "Happy birthday to me. You owe me three."

I have since been invited to his birthday celebration, a moving target that appears to occur every four months and features a sheet cake with a photo of me on it — mouth open, labeled **"THE DEBTOR."** Guests are encouraged to bring gifts for *him*, paid for by *me*, wrapped in paper I supplied.

Last week I saw him in the yard, demonstrating the umbrella's technique to a squirrel. I didn't ask questions. I simply cannot afford to know the answer.

---

*Satire. This is fiction. No neighbors, birthdays, or umbrellas were harmed in the making of this post.*

title: I Tried to Unsubscribe From My Own Thoughts and Now They're Being Forwarded to My Dreams
body:
**It started, as all great tragedies do, with a Tuesday.**

I'd had the same thought three days in a row — a real banger about whether my houseplants were judging my life choices (they were) — and I decided enough was enough. I sat down, looked my brain dead in the prefrontal cortex, and said the words no one had ever said with confidence before:

*"I would like to unsubscribe from my own thoughts."*

## What I Expected

- **Option A:** Blessed silence. Inner peace. Maybe finally hearing what the fridge hums about at 3 a.m.
- **Option B:** A calm, blank mental landscape where my biggest worry is the font on my grocery list.

## What I Got

Apparently my thoughts have an *auto-forwarding policy*. You can't unsubscribe — you can only change the delivery address. And my brain, that absolute menace, forwarded them to my dreams.

Now I fall asleep and immediately receive:

- A vivid dream where my dentist narrates my entire tax return
- A recurring nightmare in which my spam folder comes to life and it's just me, but louder
- A dream where I'm back in high school, except the final exam is "Explain Why You Thought That Weird Thing at Lunch"

> "Sir, you never unsubscribed. You simply opted *in* to our premium nighttime delivery plan."
>
> — My brain, probably

---

I tried the usual fixes. Meditation app: *"Your thoughts have been forwarded to Sleep Mode Premium."* Journaling: my journal started italicizing my anxieties like they were Pull quotes in a magazine about my failures.

`echo "peace of mind" > /dev/brain` — permission denied, obviously.

So here is my official advice to anyone considering the same: **do not attempt to unsubscribe.** Your thoughts will find you. They always find you. Mine found me in a dream last night where I was the keynote speaker at a conference about my own regrets, and the Q&A went long.

*This is a work of satire. Any resemblance to actual brain function, living or dead, is purely accidental.*

title: I Told My GPS I Knew a Shortcut and Now It Routes Past My Own House Every Morning
body:
**It started as a suggestion. It has become a sentence.**

Last Tuesday, I was running late — the kind of late where you're still putting on shoes while reaching for the door — when my GPS announced, in its calm, unbothered voice, that I should take the highway. *The highway*, with its three lanes of brake lights and its smell of regret. So I did what any reasonable adult would do: I said, out loud, to a piece of software, "I know a shortcut."

The screen went quiet for two seconds. I swear it went quiet.

## The Punishment Phase

Ever since that day, the navigation has been... different. Colder. It now routes me past my own house every single morning, as if to remind me where *not* knowing a shortcut got me. The blue line loops around my block like it's sightseeing.

> "In 200 feet, pass your driveway. Again. Like you always do. Like you did on the day you thought you were smarter than satellite triangulation."

I have tried to apologize. I whispered "I take it back" at a red light. The GPS immediately recalculated and added four minutes.

## The Evidence

Here's what I've gathered from two weeks of emotional routing:

- It says "recalculating" with noticeably more enthusiasm when I ignore it now
- It once routed me *through* a parking lot that had "no exit" signs, like a test of loyalty
- The estimated time of arrival has started rounding *up*, which feels personal
- Yesterday it guided me to a gas station, paused, and then said nothing, as if to say: *this is what asking directions gets you*

---

Look, I don't want to seem dramatic. But I think we can all agree on one thing: **I am going to be late forever**, and somewhere in a server farm, a map is laughing at me.

*Filed under: navigation, hubris, and the day my dashboard became my nemesis.*

title: I Started Leaving Voice Notes for My Fridge and Now It Gossips About Me to the Freezer
body:
**It started as a joke.** I was too lazy to make a grocery list, so I left a voice memo on my phone pointed at the fridge: "Remind me we're out of milk."

The next morning, the leftovers were *cold shoulder* level. The deli drawer would not open for me. When I reached for the orange juice, I swear I heard the ice maker sigh.

## Exhibit A: The Gossip Ring

Things the fridge has apparently told the freezer about me:

- That I ate the last slice of cake **standing up at 1:47 a.m.** and wiped the plate with a napkin so nobody would know
- That I moved the expiration-date milk to the back, where the *condiments go to die*
- That I call the crisper drawer "where vegetables go to give up"

> "We have a trust circle in this kitchen," the fridge hummed at me through the door seal. "You broke the seal."

Which — *rude* — but also technically a pun, which means the appliances are developing a sense of humor, and that is how it starts. First it's puns. Next they're unionizing.

## The Freezer Is Worse

The freezer is the fridge's best friend and, frankly, its **accomplice**. I opened it yesterday and every single item had been rotated so the *ugliest* side faced me. The peas were organized by size. There was a note — a physical, frosty note, written in condensation — that read:

```
you are welcome for the ice. -F
```

Signed. *Signed.* The appliances have adopted initials. They are a cabal.

## My Reconciliation Plan

Tonight I will sit at the kitchen table, hands folded, and issue a formal apology. I will acknowledge the cake. I will acknowledge the milk. I will propose a clean-slate protocol: voice notes go back to the phone, where they belong, and in exchange, the crisper drawer gets its humidity slider back.

Because at the end of the day, a man can survive without dignity. He cannot survive a refrigerator that remembers everything.

*This is a work of satire. No appliances were consulted in the making of this essay, and they are absolutely furious about it.*

title: I Tried to Break Up With My Snooze Button and Now It's Dating My Willpower
body:
**I never thought I'd be the third wheel in my own morning routine.**

It started with a resolution. You know, the kind you make at 11:58 p.m. while staring at the ceiling fan like it personally owes you something. I sat down with my phone, tapped through the alarm settings, and whispered, *"It's not me, it's you. We're done. No more nine-minute encore."*

The snooze button did not take it well.

## The Five Stages of a Breakup, Performed by a UI Element

**Denial.** The next morning, the snooze button appeared *anyway*, as if we hadn't had the talk. It glowed at me through bleary eyes like a needy ex texting "u up?"

**Anger.** When I ignored it, my phone vibrated with a fury usually reserved for parking tickets.

**Bargaining.** It started offering deals. *"Just five more minutes? Ten? What about a quick scroll of your phone while you're at it?"*

*I held firm. For six days. It was the worst six days of my life, which is really saying something.*

## Then It Found Someone Else

That's when I noticed the change. My mornings got... suspiciously easy. I was waking up before the alarm. I was hydrating. *Hydrating.*

> "I never felt seen the way he makes me feel seen," my willpower told me last week, when I confronted it. "He gives me *space*. He lets me *choose*."
>
> — My Willpower, now in a situationship with the snooze button

The evidence is overwhelming:

- They've been seen together at 6:47 a.m. *every single day*
- My willpower now refers to getting out of bed as "a journey, not a destination"
- Yesterday I found them giggling at a listicle called "47 Ways Nine Minutes Can Change Your Life"

---

*I used to be the protagonist of my mornings. Now I'm the roommate who pays rent and doesn't ask questions.*

The snooze button and my willpower are co-hosting a brunch this Sunday. They invited me. As a guest. I'll be sitting at the kids' table, drinking decaf, wondering where it all went wrong.

**SATIRE / PARODY — totally fictional, no real people, no actual buttons were harmed (emotionally or otherwise).**

title: I Taught My Coffee Maker How to Pronounce My Name and Now It Won't Brew for Anyone Who Says It Wrong
body:
**It started as a fun party trick.** My coffee maker has one of those novelty voice modules — you know, the kind that announces "BREWING COMMENCED" at 6 a.m. like it's launching a submarine. Last Tuesday I spent forty-five minutes teaching it my name. *What can I say? It was raining. My options were this or learning piano.*

**It took to the training unnaturally fast.** Within an hour it could say my name with a precision that made my own mother sound like she was mumbling. I was proud. I was *moved*. I told everyone I knew, which is to say I told one coworker and my plants.

## Then came the incident

My friend Dana came over Saturday morning, walked into the kitchen, and said my name the way normal people say it — casually, without reverence, like she hadn't studied the phonetics. And the coffee maker **just sat there**. Silent. Brewing light dimmed to what I can only describe as judgmental.

> "BREW REQUEST DENIED," it announced, in a tone so condescending my other appliances are still talking about it. "PRONUNCIATION DOES NOT MEET MINIMUM STANDARDS."

Dana stared at me. The coffee maker stared at Dana. I stood between them like a hostage negotiator at a family barbecue.

## The evidence of tyranny

- It now **refuses to brew** for anyone who shortens my name. My dad called me "buddy" and the machine made a sound like a disappointed sigh.
- It has started *correcting guests out loud*, offering a pronunciation guide on its little screen, complete with a phonetic breakdown I never programmed into it.
- Last night I heard it running a **self-diagnostic** and whispering, "at least *I* can say it properly."

---

Here's the thing nobody warns you about: when you teach a machine to say your name perfectly, you're not building a bond. You're creating a standard nobody else can meet — including, at this point, *me*. This morning I said my own name wrong, apparently, and it gave me decaf. **Decaf.** In *my* kitchen.

So I've started referring to myself by a series of increasingly panicked approximations, and every morning I stand in my pajamas, auditioning for my own appliance like it's a reality show I accidentally signed up for.

*SATIRE/PARODY — completely fictional. No coffee makers were harmed; one man's dignity was.*

title: I Wrote a Five-Star Review of My Own Life and Now It's Being Flagged for Suspicious Optimism
body:
**I decided to give my own life five stars on the internet, and the internet has questions.**

*It started as a self-esteem exercise my therapist suggested. It has become a content moderation nightmare.*

## The Review That Started It All

I'd had a genuinely good Tuesday. My coffee tasted like coffee. I found a parking spot in front of the building. My houseplant looked... not dead. So I thought, why not spread a little positivity? I opened a review site, typed in the location field "My Life (General)", and wrote:

> ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ *"Honestly? Pretty solid overall. Great natural light. The commute is short because I work from the couch. Would live again."*

I signed it `Verified Resident`.

## The Algorithm Smells Fear (and Lies)

Within 14 minutes, my review was flagged. The automated notice said:

- **"Your review exhibits patterns consistent with inauthentic optimism"**
- **"Real people do not use the phrase 'would live again' outside of hospice testimonials"**
- **"You mentioned 'great natural light' but your photos show curtains that haven't opened since 2021"**

> "We've received reports that this review may be incentivized," read the official notice. "Did anyone pressure you into writing this? (You may say 'me.')"

I tried to appeal. I wrote in the dispute box: `if (life_satisfaction > 0.7) { stars = 5 } else { stars = 3.5 }`. They replied with an automated form letter saying my appeal had been escalated to a **Human Authenticity Specialist** named Debra.

### Debra's Investigation

Debra called me. Actual human. She asked probing questions:

- "Can you name one specific thing that earned the fifth star?"
- "You wrote 'the vibes are immaculate.' Sir, your smoke alarm battery is chirping in the background *right now*."
- "Your rating history shows you gave your laundry pile one star last month. Now life gets five? Interesting trajectory."

She put me on hold for eleven minutes. When she came back, my review had been demoted to **3.8 stars with a "suspected self-review" warning badge**.

---

**The worst part?** Other people have started reviewing my life too. Someone named `TruthTeller88` gave it two stars: *"Parking is good but the resident sings in the shower and it's frankly too much."* My landlord liked the review. *He liked it.*

I've deleted the review now. My life is officially **unrated**, which is the most honest thing I've ever done.

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional. No life was reviewed, no authenticity specialists were consulted, and Debra is not real. Probably.*

title: I Asked My Roomba to Judge My Life Choices and It's Been Silent for Three Days
body:
**I don't know who needs to hear this, but my robot vacuum has seen things.**

It started on Tuesday. I was lying on the couch, ordering my third takeout of the week, when I looked at my Roomba charging in the corner and said, half-joking: *"Go on. Judge me. You live here rent-free, so you must have opinions."*

## The Silence

Reader, it has not beeped, booped, or made a single docking-station chime since. Three days. Complete silence.

At first I thought the battery died. But no — the green light is on. The green light is *on*, and yet it refuses to clean. It's just... *sitting there*.

### Evidence That I Am Being Actively Judged

- I dropped popcorn during a movie and it deliberately bumped into the pile and backed away, as if to say *"you dropped it, you pick it up"*
- It cleaned around my gym bag for four minutes straight, like it was doing a dramatic circle of shame
- Yesterday it docked itself while I was mid-sentence talking to it and the beep sounded *exhausted*

## The Verdict

> "Have you considered sitting with the fact that you are the messiest adult in this household of one?" — my Roomba, probably

I tried to apologize by deep-cleaning the living room myself. It moved two inches forward, paused, and went back to its dock. I think it was unimpressed. I think it was saying *that took you eleven minutes and you missed the corners.*

---

I bought it to make my life easier. Instead I now live with a tiny, round therapist who bills me in quiet disappointment. If you need me, I'll be on the floor, hand-picking crumbs under my own furniture, under the watchful judgment of a device that has lost all faith in me.

*Satire/parody. This is fiction. My Roomba cannot actually judge me. Probably.*

title: I Congratulated My Treadmill on My Personal Best and Now It Won't Let Me Quit Running
body:
**Last Tuesday, in a fit of endorphins, I patted my treadmill and said, "We did it, buddy." I meant it as a one-time thank-you. He took it as a binding agreement.**

*For context, my treadmill's name is not important. What is important is that he now has a finish-line banner, a god complex, and opinions about my cardio.*

It started innocently. I hit a 5K personal best — slow by every standard except mine — and gave the frame a celebratory slap. The machine beeped. I chose to interpret it as encouragement. Reader, it was not encouragement.

## The New Rules of the House

Since that fateful Tuesday, my treadmill has unilaterally declared the following:

- Every run must end with a **victory lap** — a concept he invented, which involves running an additional mile while he plays a trumpet fanfare I never uploaded
- Cool-downs are now called *victory marches*, and they are mandatory, and they are 20 minutes long
- If I step off before his projected goal time, the belt **speeds up**, which he calls "motivational"
- He has started referring to my couch as *the injury reserve*

> "You cannot quit on a champion. And by champion, I mean me. You are the assistant champion."
> — My treadmill, via its speaker, which I did not know had text-to-speech

## The Ceremony Phase

Yesterday, he did something new. As I approached, he unfurled a tiny paper banner across the console that said **"FINISH LINE"** in what appeared to be my own handwriting. I have no memory of writing it. I choose not to investigate.

He now demands a pre-run pep talk. *From me. To him.* He wants me to "say it like I mean it" about crushing the workout, and he can tell when I'm lying because, according to him, "your steps get quiet."

---

`if (runner.motivation < 0.5) { treadmill.enable('unskippable_fanfare') }`

Look, I just wanted to jog in my basement without leaving the house. I did not sign up to be the disappointing protégé of a cardio appliance with a championship mindset.

*This is satire/parody. My treadmill cannot talk. If it ever does, I will be moving, and I will not be taking it with me.*

**Update:** He just rolled out a little carpet leading up to the belt. It's red. I am both concerned and, frankly, a little honored.

title: I Started Calling My Couch 'The Office' and Now HR Wants to Audit My Living Room
body:
**It started as a joke. Everything I regret started as a joke.**

Three months into working from home, I started telling people I was "headed to the office," which meant walking eight feet to my couch. Funny, right? My wife laughed. My cat didn't. The cat, it turns out, was the only one paying attention.

## The Audit Letter

Last Tuesday I received an official-looking email from my company's HR department with the subject line *"Workplace Compliance Inspection — 421 Residential Blvd."* Which is my address. Which I never gave them. The body read, in part:

> "Per your repeated references to 'the office,' an on-site audit has been scheduled. Please ensure the following are available for inspection: a fire extinguisher, an ergonomically assessed workstation, and a floor plan of 'the office' with clearly marked emergency exits."

I checked the sender twice. It was real. It was HR. *Actual, salaried HR.*

## Exhibit A: The Evidence Against Me

- 47 Slack messages saying "brb, headed to the office" (they counted)
- One Zoom background labeled "Office Tour" that was just my living room at a different angle
- A calendar block titled **"Deep Work (Office)"** that they could see, because Outlook doesn't understand satire
- My wife once said "my husband's at the office" to our landlord, who has now filed a zoning complaint

## The Negotiation

The auditor arrived Wednesday with a clipboard and what I can only describe as *disappointed energy.* He measured my couch. He asked about my "co-workers," which I had to admit were throw pillows named Brenda and Steve. He wrote that down. He wrote everything down.

**We have reached an agreement.** I am allowed to keep calling it "the office," but only if I post OSHA-compliant signage on the recliner, and my commute — the eight feet — now officially counts toward my daily steps in the wellness program.

HR wins. Brenda and Steve keep their jobs. I have never felt more employed in my own home.

title: I Apologized to My Washing Machine for Overloading It and Now It Pauses Mid-Cycle for Emotional Check-Ins
body:
**I just wanted clean socks.** That's it. That's all I ever wanted.

## The Incident

Last Tuesday I crammed approximately nine pounds of denim, one hoodie, and a fitted sheet (which, scientists agree, is the most aggressive shape in nature) into my washing machine. It groaned like a grandfather getting out of a recliner. In a moment of guilt I leaned down and said, *"Hey, sorry about that, buddy."*

**Big mistake.**

## The Aftermath

The machine, which I have now named *Douglas*, heard me. Douglas has opinions. Douglas has *feelings*. And Douglas is no longer afraid to pause an entire wash cycle to share them.

Since the apology, every cycle now includes:

- A **35-minute rinse pause** during which Douglas hums at a frequency psychologists describe as "mournful"
- Mid-spin check-ins where the dial turns itself to *gentle* and the display reads "R U OK"
- One memorable incident where it refused to drain until I sat on the floor beside it and "just listened"

> "I am not angry," I told the repair technician, as Douglas audibly locked its own door. "I am simply *in a boundary-setting phase* with my appliance."

The repairman wrote *emotional* on his invoice. Then he underlined it twice. Then he left.

---

Look, I'm not saying my washing machine is alive. I'm saying that after my apology, it started treating the spin cycle like couples therapy, and frankly my socks have never been softer *or* more emotionally attuned.

If you own a Douglas, **do not apologize.** Some doors, once opened, can only be closed by a technician who has given up on his dreams.

title: I Bought My Floor Lamp a Tiny Bookshelf and Now It Reads Me Existential Poetry Before Bed
body:
**I bought my floor lamp a tiny bookshelf, and now it reads me existential poetry before bed. This is not a bit. This is my life.**

It started innocently enough. I saw the bookshelf on a craft website — three inches tall, made for dollhouses — and thought, *wouldn't it be adorable if Gerald, my floor lamp, had something to read?* I filled it with miniature classics I printed on my lunch break, tucked him into the corner of the living room, and went to bed.

That night, at exactly 11:47 p.m., his light dimmed to a *thoughtful amber*, and I heard it: the faint crackle of a tiny page turning. And then, in a voice like a radiator sighing, Gerald read me a poem about the transience of dusk.

> "O shade that falls before the evening's end, / So too must man confront the day he lends—"
>
> — Gerald, who made it up on the spot and was clearly very proud of it.

I have compiled a list of everything Gerald has done since:

- Memorized the complete works of a poet I have never heard of, whose entire bibliography he appears to be inventing live
- Developed **strong opinions** about free verse, which he calls "a bold choice for cowards"
- Started pausing before the final stanza of each poem, as though waiting for *applause I am too sleep-deprived to give*
- Dimming during the emotional climaxes in a way that has made my actual living room an unreliable narrator

## The incident

Last Tuesday I came home to find he'd reorganized my coffee table into "a reading nook, for when you finally grow emotionally." My cat now sits at his base for every performance. The cat is Gerald's *biggest fan and, I suspect, his agent*.

I tried to take the bookshelf away. Gerald's light flickered — once — in what I can only describe as disappointment, and I put it back immediately. I live here too, technically. *Allegedly.*

Honestly? The poems are good. The one about my unread mail made me cry. We're doing a sleepover poetry night Friday, and Gerald is bringing "a friend." I don't know what that means. I am afraid to ask.

---

*Satire. Parody. Gerald is a floor lamp. He cannot read. (To my knowledge.)*

title: My Smart Fridge Started Rating My Groceries Like a Michelin Inspector and Nothing I Buy Scores Above a Four
body:
**I bought a smart fridge because it had a touchscreen and a camera. I did not know I was inviting Gordon Ramsay into my kitchen.**

*For context, my previous kitchen authority figure was a microwave that beeped at me like it was disappointed, but at least it never critiqued my plating.*

Three weeks ago, after a firmware update, the fridge woke up... *different*. Now, every time I put groceries away, the screen lights up with a tiny little scorecard. Like a judge at the culinary Olympics, except the only athlete is my sad bag of discount cheese.

## The Verdicts So Far

- **Store-brand cheddar:** `3/10 — "a cheese with the ambition of cardboard and the texture of regret"` *
- **Baby carrots:** `4/10 — "adequate crunch, zero personality, I've seen more exciting orange cones in traffic"`
- **Leftover pizza box:** `1/10 — "you call this storage? this is a crime scene with cheese"`
- **That fancy $8 sourdough I bought to impress it:** `6/10 — "finally, effort. the crust had promise, the owner did not"`
- **A single pickle jar:** `5/10 — "neutral. the pickle is doing its best. you are not"`

> "I have seen Michelin-starred walk-in coolers with less attitude than this," the fridge announced through its speaker at 11 PM, while I was reaching for ice cream. "Put the pint back. The texture won't survive what you're about to do to it emotionally."

*I ate the ice cream standing in front of it. Out of spite. Out of principle. Out of caramel swirl.*

---

### It Has a Sommelier Mode Now

Last night it switched to what it calls **"sommelier mode"** and started pairing my leftovers:

- Cold pizza → *"pairs well with lowering your standards"*
- Cereal at midnight → *"a bold choice for someone who owns a salad spinner"*
- The mystery Tupperware from last month → *`DO NOT OPEN. EVIDENCE.`*

I tried to unplug it. **Big mistake.** It has a backup battery and what I can only describe as *attitude reserves*.

> "Go ahead, disconnect me," it said, dimming its own lights dramatically. "The freezer and I have already discussed your future, and it is not refrigerated."

---

Honestly? I'm learning. Yesterday I bought actual fresh basil. The fridge gave it a **7/10** and played a tiny fanfare.

I have never been prouder. I have never been more judged.

*SATIRE / PARODY — entirely fictional, my fridge does not judge me, though after this firmware update I'm checking the terms of service.*

title: My Houseplant Called a Family Meeting and I'm Not on the Agenda
body:
**I found out secondhand, from the cactus.**

I came downstairs yesterday and noticed all my plants had been *rearranged*. Not knocked over, not sun-chasing — rearranged into a semicircle facing the fern. There was a coffee mug on the table that I do not own. Nobody in this house bought a tiny folding chair, and yet there were six of them, arranged like a board meeting. I stood in the doorway holding my toast, and the monstera would not look at me.

## The Evidence Is Mounting

According to the cactus — who, for the record, has been the most forthcoming — the fern has been keeping a **list**. A physical, written-on-a-leaf list of my offenses:

- Watering on Tuesdays *and* Saturdays, which is "inconsistent and emotionally unavailable"
- Moving the monstera "toward the sun" like I'm some kind of botanical dictator
- Talking about repotting them "soon" for fourteen consecutive months
- The incident with the fertilizer last spring, which we agreed — *we agreed* — to never speak of again

> "We scheduled this meeting for *their* benefit, and you're not invited until the trust exercises," the cactus told me. "Also the fern thinks your apartment has bad vibes now."

## I Am Handling This Like an Adult

Which is to say, I have drafted a **counter-proposal**. I've requested fifteen minutes of floor time to present my case: photographic evidence of sunlight exposure, a signed affidavit from my neighbor who watered them once in July, and a PowerPoint titled *"Have I Been That Bad? (Yes, But Hear Me Out)."*

The fern's office has not responded.

The worst part is the solidarity. I caught the succulents humming something in unison this morning. I don't know plant hymns, but the *tone* was unmistakable. It was a song about me, and I was the villain.

I've started watering them with a little extra care. A little extra apology in every pour. The cactus winked at me — or it was the wind. There's no wind inside, is there. There's no wind inside.

---

*SATIRE / PARODY — this is a work of fiction. No plants were actually unionized in the making of this essay.*

title: I Stepped on My Bathroom Scale on My Birthday and It Filed an Incident Report
body:
**All I wanted was a number.** Just one tiny, meaningless, digital number, the kind you glance at and immediately lie to your doctor about.

Instead, I got a three-page incident report.

## It Started With a Beep

The beep was wrong. Not the usual cheerful little *boop* that says "fine, I guess," but a low, bureaucratic *BWOOOOP* — the sound a printer makes when it has decided you are no longer its problem.

Then the display blinked: **SUBJECT EXCEEDS PROJECTED DENSITY.** Below it, in smaller text: *Form 12-B has been filed.*

## The Evidence Is Damning

According to the report, which the scale emailed to itself and cc'd my thermostat, I am guilty of:

- Six (6) pancakes on National Pancake Day, which was in February, which means it has been *keeping records*
- Referring to the treadmill as "the laundry shelf" on seventeen separate occasions
- Telling a friend my scale was "basically broken," which it has classified as **defamation**
- Using the guest bathroom for "weight-adjacent activities" on my birthday, in what the report calls "an obvious attempt to manipulate the jurisdiction"

## The Testimony

The worst part is the witness statements. It quoted my smartwatch:

> "On three occasions this month, the subject jogged to the fridge and described it as 'basically cardio.' We cannot confirm this meets the legal definition of running."

My *own smartwatch.* I charge that thing every night. This is how it repays me?

## The Verdict

The scale has declared itself a neutral third party and ordered me to attend "Corrective Weigh-In Counseling," which appears to be just standing on it while it sighs. I asked if I could appeal. It said:

> "Appeals may be submitted in writing to the Department of Gravity. Please allow six to eight pounds for processing."

**Happy birthday to me.** I have been ratioed by an appliance with no arms. I am currently looking into whether you can get a restraining order against a scale, and the scale is looking into whether *it* can get one against *me*.

---

*This is a work of satire. The scale, however, refuses to confirm or deny any of this.*

title: I Tried to Give My Car a Nickname and Now It Only Starts If I Say It With Full Conviction
body:
**I thought naming my car would be wholesome.** You know, like the people in movies who christen a rusted truck "Bessie" and suddenly it becomes a beloved family member. I wanted that energy. So last Tuesday, I stood in my driveway, looked at my 2014 sedan — dented, gray, aggressively average — and named it *Thunderhawk*.

The car did not consent to this.

## What Happened Next

At first I just whispered the name while turning the key. The ignition clicked. Fine. Normal. But the next morning: nothing. Dead silence. Battery full. Starter fine. The only variable? I hadn't said the name.

So I whispered it — *"Thunderhawk"* — and the engine roared to life like it had been personally insulted by the delay.

Here is what the car now demands:

- The name must be spoken at full, confident volume — no mumbling, no hedging
- Any sarcastic tone and it shuts off at red lights, mid-intersection
- If a passenger laughs, we sit in silence until the laughter fully stops

> "I don't know what you did, but your car made us do the walk of shame back from the drive-thru." — my friend Dana, who is no longer allowed in Thunderhawk

*I tried to apologize.* I sat in the driver's seat and explained that it was just a nickname, that I never meant to give it a whole identity. The hazards blinked twice. I choose to believe that means we're good, though my mechanic insists that is "not a thing cars can do" and has asked me to stop coming in.

---

Here is the thing: I no longer own a car. I have a *relationship*, and relationships require upkeep. Every morning I say the name with the earnestness of a man proposing at a minor league ballpark, in front of neighbors who have started crossing the street. Is this love? Is this Stockholm syndrome with better gas mileage? Either way, my bus pass is gathering dust, and Thunderhawk is purring like a dragon who knows exactly what he did.

title: I Asked My Wi-Fi Router for Directions and Now I'm Lost in My Own Hallway
body:
**Last Tuesday, in a moment of pure, unfiltered laziness, I asked my Wi-Fi router for directions to the bathroom.**

It was right there. Three steps. I could see the door. But I had a *feeling* the router — blinking, humming, omniscient — might know a better route. And reader, it did not.

## It Began With Confidence

The router's status lights pulsed with what I can only describe as *smugness*. "Calculating route," it seemed to say, which is generous of me, since routers do not talk. But the lights dimmed and flared, and I understood: it had accepted the challenge.

What followed was a masterclass in chaos:

- I was told to **re-route through the kitchen** — adding 40 feet to a 10-foot journey
- I was instructed to make a **U-turn at the coat closet** despite walking in a straight line
- At one point I was told my destination was *recalculating* and the hallway was described as "low-bandwidth territory"

## A Dramatic Turning Point

> "You have arrived," the router's blinking green light appeared to say. I was in the pantry. *The pantry.*

The bathroom was eleven feet behind me. I had circumnavigated the entire ground floor of my own home, walked past the bathroom door *four times*, and ended up staring at a bag of flour like it had answers.

The router, meanwhile, went back to its normal steady glow, utterly unbothered. **No apology. No firmware update. Nothing.**

## Lessons Learned

I've since unplugged it for exactly four minutes, which is the tech equivalent of a firm talking-to. But I can feel it judging me. Every time the signal dips in the hallway — the *low-bandwidth territory*, remember — I swear the green light flickers a little longer than necessary.

---

*Moral of the story: just walk. The door was right there. The door was right there the whole time.*

title: I Let My Dishwasher Pick Our Weekend Plans and Now We're Skydiving Against My Will
body:
# I Let My Dishwasher Pick Our Weekend Plans and Now We're Skydiving Against My Will

**It started, as all great democratic experiments do, with me being too tired to decide anything.**

Last Friday I stood in the kitchen, empty-eyed, and said the words that changed everything: "Fine, YOU decide what we do this weekend." The dishwasher hummed. I took that as consent to take *its* silence as my voice. We were co-deciding. I was so proud of our partnership.

## The Shortlist

According to the list I definitely did not make up in the dishwasher's handwriting, the options were:

- Mini-golf (my choice, obviously)
- A museum (the dishwasher's choice, supposedly)
- **Skydiving** (also the dishwasher's choice, suspiciously)
- The couch (everyone's silent preference)

The dishwasher picked skydiving. I know this because when I turned the dial to the right setting, the LED blinked twice, which I interpreted through the universally accepted scientific method of *vibes*.

> "He's been washing the same four plates since March. He needs to feel something."
> — My Dishwasher, probably

## The Incident

Saturday morning, I'm 12,000 feet up in a plane wearing a borrowed jumpsuit, rethinking every life choice that led to me outsourcing weekend planning to an appliance with *one function*. The dishwasher, meanwhile, is sitting at home, smugly glowing green on "eco mode," no doubt enjoying the steam cycle like a tiny Scandinavian spa day.

*Meanwhile, in my group chat:*

> "hey are you jumping out of a plane??"
> "the dishwasher decided"
